title: Hermes Consultant Advanced: Practice Exam
description: Timed practice exam covering the whole series. Pass with 72% or higher to earn the course completion certificate.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Setting Up a Consultancy: Legal, Finance, Tooling, and Operations”, what is the core reason for forming a legal entity rather than contracting as an individual?
options: To reduce the tax the practice pays on consulting income.
To separate the practice's obligations from the person's, so the company can be liable without the founder losing personal assets.
To make invoicing simpler for enterprise clients.
To allow the practice to hire contractors without a written agreement.
questions.explanation: The lesson says that without an entity every contract, dispute, and judgment lands on the person, and that separation is the whole reason the entity exists.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: The lesson says only technical staff should act on this.
The lesson states this is never a relevant consideration.
The discipline is to make the unit small enough to finish in a bounded window and explicit enough that a different agent could take it over mid-flight without losing context.
The discipline is not to make the unit small enough to finish in a bounded window and explicit enough that a different agent could take it over mid-flight without losing context.
questions.explanation: The discipline is to make the unit small enough to finish in a bounded window and explicit enough that a different agent could take it over mid-flight without losing context.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Setting Up a Consultancy: Legal, Finance, Tooling, and Operations”, what does the lesson say about ownership of the practice's functions?
options: Every function has to have a named owner, so that when a person leaves their functions are already named and can be reassigned.
The principal should own every function until the practice can afford a dedicated operator for it.
Ownership can be implicit as long as the team is small and communicates well.
Only the reference architectures and internal tooling need named owners.
questions.explanation: The lesson says a practice where ownership is implicit is one departure away from discovering it did not actually know how its own firm ran.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Case Study: Scaling a Practice from Solo to Team”, what is the real unit of scaling?
options: The distance between the principal and any work product that crosses the client threshold, measured by how many current products would degrade if the principal vanished tomorrow.
Annual revenue growth, since that is what funds the next hire.
Headcount, because a larger team can carry more concurrent engagements.
The number of signed engagements per quarter.
questions.explanation: The lesson says a practice with twelve employees is usually still a solo practice with twelve employees if every deliverable still passes through one head to be trusted.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Delivery Operations: Utilization, Capacity, and Margins”, why does the lesson call 100 percent utilization a warning rather than a win?
options: Because clients expect a practice to keep some capacity reserved for their competitors.
Because slack is the buffer that lets the system absorb the unexpected, and with none every new demand becomes a queue that shows up later as rework and burnout.
Because utilization above 80 percent always means the denominator was defined too generously.
Because billable work is less profitable than internal IP capture work.
questions.explanation: The lesson says slack is not waste but the buffer that keeps the system responsive, and the cost of over-utilization appears weeks later where that number does not track it.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson’s guidance?
options: Lesson 1 ended with a test: you are a principal the day a client gets a good result and you were not the one who made it.
The lesson cautions against this in every real-world case.
Lesson 1 ended with a test: you is not a principal the day a client gets a good result and you were not the one who made it.
The lesson says only technical staff should act on this.
questions.explanation: Lesson 1 ended with a test: you are a principal the day a client gets a good result and you were not the one who made it.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Scoping, Defending, and Closing the Consulting Sale”, where is most scope creep actually prevented?
options: In change control, once the engagement is underway and the requests arrive.
In the proposal, by naming every deliverable, assumption, and exclusion so the boundary is honest from the start.
In the contract, by reserving the right to re-price any new request.
In delivery, by absorbing small requests so the client stays happy.
questions.explanation: The lesson says scope creep is usually a scoping failure baked in before signing, and genuine changes after a tight scope are handled as change requests with a re-estimate.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Hiring, Onboarding, and Running a Team of Consultants”, what is the central focus?
options: The principal hires for the delivery system, not for a role they used to fill. How to staff against a captured method, onboard people onto it with a measurable exit gate, and run a team so quality stays a property of the system instead of a bet on any single person.
A history of the technology and its vendors
A review of unrelated productivity tools
A summary of corporate policy rules
questions.explanation: The lesson is centered on: The principal hires for the delivery system, not for a role they used to fill. How to staff against a captured method, onboard people onto it with a measurable exit gate, and run a team so quality stays a property of the system instead of a bet on any single person.

questions.question: Per the lesson “From Consultant to Principal”, what is the central focus?
options: The shift that defines a principal: from selling your own skill to building a delivery system. Why the unit of output changes, how leverage replaces hours, and what you have to stop doing to operate at scale.
A history of the technology and its vendors
A review of unrelated productivity tools
A summary of corporate policy rules
questions.explanation: The lesson is centered on: The shift that defines a principal: from selling your own skill to building a delivery system. Why the unit of output changes, how leverage replaces hours, and what you have to stop doing to operate at scale.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Design Authority”, what is the central focus?
options: The layer that keeps a growing practice coherent. What design authority is, why a system of many agents drifts without it, how to set standards that actually get followed, and how to run design reviews that are gates, not rubber stamps.
A history of the technology and its vendors
A review of unrelated productivity tools
A summary of corporate policy rules
questions.explanation: The lesson is centered on: The layer that keeps a growing practice coherent. What design authority is, why a system of many agents drifts without it, how to set standards that actually get followed, and how to run design reviews that are gates, not rubber stamps.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Pricing Strategy: From Hourly to Productized to Value-Based”, what structure does the lesson recommend for a value-based deal?
options: A floor that covers delivery cost and baseline margin, plus a share of the measured value above the baseline, never a pure contingency.
A pure contingency fee so the practice's interests align fully with the client's.
A fixed price set by reverse-engineering the estimated hours at the practice's rate.
An hourly rate with a success bonus paid at the client's discretion.
questions.explanation: The lesson says a pure value-based fee converts the delivery system into an unfunded speculation, while the floor keeps the practice solvent on the work itself.

questions.question: Per the lesson “The Financial Model: Units, Margins, and Runway”, what distinction does the lesson draw between modeling and forecasting?
options: Keep the model rigorous, the prices, costs, contributions, fixed base, and runway formula, and keep the forecast humble, since the forecast is always wrong in the details.
Model monthly and forecast annually, because yearly forecasts are more accurate.
Model the units and forecast the runway, because runway cannot be modeled.
Model conservatively and forecast optimistically so the firm is not under-investing.
questions.explanation: The lesson says to spend attention on the structure you control rather than pretending the revenue forecast is precise.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Pricing Strategy: From Hourly to Productized to Value-Based”, why is hourly pricing a trap for a practice that has captured IP?
options: Because hourly rates are always lower than value-based fees for the same work.
Because clients refuse to sign hourly contracts for agent-delivered work.
Because hourly rewards slowness, so every efficiency that makes delivery cheaper under captured IP also produces a smaller bill.
Because hourly pricing prevents the practice from forecasting utilization.
questions.explanation: The lesson says a practice has built an efficiency machine and priced itself to lose the moment it works.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Scoping, Defending, and Closing the Consulting Sale”, how do the estimate and the price relate?
options: The estimate is an internal fact-finding question against your own method, while the price is an external value judgment in the market, informed by the estimate but not equal to it.
The price is the estimate plus a standard markup chosen by the practice.
The estimate should be set to equal the price so the delivery team is protected.
The price is the estimate discounted by whatever the buyer's budget allows.
questions.explanation: The lesson says the estimate is the floor below which you subsidize the client and the value is the ceiling the buyer will tolerate, with the price chosen deliberately between them.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Scoping, Defending, and Closing the Consulting Sale”, a CFO challenges the price and says three other vendors quoted less. What should the principal do?
options: Offer a discount to keep the deal alive, since a lost deal costs more than a thinner margin.
Explain that the other vendors are not credible and ask the CFO to disregard them.
Reduce the scope silently to fit the lower price without telling the buyer.
Return to the value: restate what changes, what it is worth, and what it costs the buyer not to act, because discounting without re-establishing value teaches the buyer the price was arbitrary.
questions.explanation: The lesson says a price challenge usually means the buyer does not yet see the value, not that the number is too high in the abstract.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson’s guidance?
options: Lesson 2 taught you to turn capability into offers, and Lesson 4 taught you to keep the delivery system coherent with standards and review.
The opposite is true: lesson 2 taught you to turn capability into offers, and Lesson 4 taught you to keep the delivery system coherent with standards and review.
The lesson cautions against this in every real-world case.
The lesson advises ignoring this entirely in practice.
questions.explanation: Lesson 2 taught you to turn capability into offers, and Lesson 4 taught you to keep the delivery system coherent with standards and review.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Capstone, Build a Complete Go-to-Market Plan for Your Own Practice”, what test does the capstone give for telling a go-to-market plan from an aspiration?
options: Whether the plan has been approved by an advisor outside the practice.
Whether every section names a target revenue number and a date to hit it.
Whether you can hand the document to a competent person who knows nothing about the practice and have them run it for a quarter.
Whether the plan includes both inbound and outbound motions in equal measure.
questions.explanation: The lesson says a plan is executable by someone other than its author; if a section reads as a resolution rather than a decision, it is an aspiration.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Quality Systems and Certification for Your Practice”, a practice wants ISO 27001 because a large prospect named it as a requirement. What does the lesson advise?
options: Pursue every major certification so the practice can answer any procurement question.
Skip certification entirely and rely on the session trail and records as evidence.
Build the system because it makes the work better, then certify because a real buyer gates on it, and ask prospects what their procurement actually requires.
Buy the certificate first so the practice can bid on work while the system catches up.
questions.explanation: The lesson says a certificate no buyer requires is a cost with no revenue attached, and certification theatre fails because an auditor's sample exposes missing records.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Managing a Client Portfolio Strategically”, why is the unit of analysis for portfolio management the account rather than the engagement?
options: Because accounts are billed monthly while engagements are billed on milestones.
Because the levers cross engagement boundaries, since you expand, renew, or decide on the whole relationship, which needs an owner accountable for more than the deliverable in flight.
Because clients insist on a single point of contact for commercial questions.
Because engagement-level data is not available in the delivery system.
questions.explanation: The lesson says managing at the account level means tracking the relationship's trajectory, not just the health of the current engagement.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Governance for Large Engagements”, why must the status cadence run on a fixed schedule even when there is no news?
options: Because clients contractually require a report every period regardless of content.
Because an activity log builds the committee's confidence in the delivery team.
Because a no-news report that always arrives and tells the truth is what makes bad news travel fast and be believed when it is flagged.
Because the report is the only artifact that makes a decision auditable after the fact.
questions.explanation: The lesson calls cadence trust engineering: if a report only appears when there is a problem, its arrival becomes a crisis signal and routine ones get ignored.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson’s guidance?
options: The opposite is true: levels 1 and 2 taught you to run engagements.
The lesson states this is never a relevant consideration.
The lesson claims this cannot be verified at all.
Levels 1 and 2 taught you to run engagements.
questions.explanation: Levels 1 and 2 taught you to run engagements.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Case Study: Scaling a Practice from Solo to Team”, why must the three separations happen in order?
options: Because the review gate cannot be built until there is a second seller to fund it.
Because the offer cannot be detached from the founder until the standard is certified.
Because a firm that builds a second seller before a second reviewer can sell more work than it can safely deliver, and the extra revenue funds a quality collapse.
Because capacity cannot be separated from the calendar until the founder stops billing.
questions.explanation: The lesson says each separation depends on the one before it, and separations built out of order fail.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: The lesson claims this cannot be verified at all.
The lesson says the opposite: this should always be avoided.
Codification is turning the judgment you use to do the work into a repeatable system that a competent person can run without you in the room.
Codification is not turning the judgment you use to do the work into a repeatable system that a competent person can run without you in the room.
questions.explanation: Codification is turning the judgment you use to do the work into a repeatable system that a competent person can run without you in the room.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Case Study: Scaling a Practice from Solo to Team”, a principal can spend the next quarter personally running one more flagship engagement, or building a third lead and packaging a new service line. How should the options be compared?
options: On revenue, because the flagship engagement funds the development later.
On the principal's own utilization, because that is the scarce resource.
On client satisfaction, because the flagship account is the firm's reputation.
On distance moved: which option increases the work the system can carry without the principal in the path, even though the busy option wins on revenue.
questions.explanation: The lesson says revenue grows under the busy option while the distance metric does not move, which is how a firm grows revenue while remaining a solo practice.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson’s guidance?
options: A principal sells capacity, wins through leverage, and turns capability into packaged offers.
The lesson argues this applies only in unrelated settings.
The lesson advises ignoring this entirely in practice.
The opposite is true: a principal sells capacity, wins through leverage, and turns capability into packaged offers.
questions.explanation: A principal sells capacity, wins through leverage, and turns capability into packaged offers.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Delivery Operations: Utilization, Capacity, and Margins”, a scheduled operating review shows utilization at 95 percent, every workstream slot occupied, and throughput flat for a month. What should the principal conclude and do?
options: Add more workstreams so the practice can keep feeding the system.
Raise the price of every offer until demand matches capacity.
Accept that flat throughput is the ceiling and stop selling for a quarter.
The binding constraint is saturated, so growth money goes at the constraint, and intake may need to slow until it clears.
questions.explanation: The lesson says adding capacity below the constraint only lengthens the queue, which shows up as high utilization with flat throughput.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Capstone, Build a Complete Go-to-Market Plan for Your Own Practice”, the plan says every part of a go-to-market plan is a decision. What does deciding mean there?
options: Choosing the marketing automation the practice will run the plan on.
A commitment that closes off alternatives, such as naming a segment deciding whom you will deliberately not pursue.
Setting a quarterly revenue target that the team is accountable to.
Selecting which competitor the practice will position against.
questions.explanation: The lesson says a section that does not close off an alternative is an aspiration and will not survive a quarter of real operations.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Managing a Client Portfolio Strategically”, what is the strategic test for whether an expansion genuinely improves the portfolio?
options: Reuse: whether the next engagement can lean on the skills, templates, and method already captured, so marginal cost falls and margin rises.
Whether the account will pay a higher rate for the second engagement than the first.
Whether the expansion keeps the delivery team at full utilization.
Whether the expansion is larger in revenue than the engagement it follows.
questions.explanation: The lesson says an account that pulls the team into a brand-new domain is expansion only in name, closer to new business wearing familiar clothes.

questions.question: Per the lesson “The Financial Model: Units, Margins, and Runway”, why should a practice model at the unit level instead of in annual revenue and profit?
options: Because yearly totals hide the fixed costs that unit modeling exposes.
Because the unit is where the levers live, a single price, a single delivery cost, a single sales volume, which is what lets the model answer what-if questions.
Because unit economics are required by lenders before a practice can raise cash.
Because annual profit is too volatile to be modeled at all.
questions.explanation: The lesson says you cannot act directly on annual profit, but you can act on one unit's price, cost, or volume, which is what the model is built to test.

questions.question: Per the lesson “The Financial Model: Units, Margins, and Runway”, Delta Forge shows healthy per-unit contribution and a practice margin of about 142,000 a year, but a stress-case runway of only about 4.8 months. What is the founder's correct first job?
options: Build a fourth rung of the ladder, since the healthy margin proves the firm can afford it.
Raise the price of the flagship build so the buffer grows faster.
Cut the fixed base below the six-month line by letting a lead go.
Bank a larger cash buffer and book retained, recurring units that lower net burn, because below the runway floor the compounding choice is not affordable.
questions.explanation: The lesson concludes that margin is the fuel and runway is the tank, so the founder must refill the tank before spending the fuel on a non-delivery bet.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Long-Term Client Partnerships and Recurring Revenue”, what is the danger the lesson names for a retainer that is a block of hours the client can burn on whatever they choose?
options: It exposes the practice to unlimited scope risk with no ceiling.
It degrades into a subscription for the client's own time management, which is selling time with extra steps and none of the transparency of time-and-materials.
It makes the recurring revenue unpredictable for both sides.
It prevents the practice from charging a value-based premium later.
questions.explanation: The lesson says a durable retainer is tied to outcomes or a delivery cadence the client can feel, not to a pool of hours.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Long-Term Client Partnerships and Recurring Revenue”, what is the tell of a real partnership rather than a vendor relationship?
options: The client renews the contract without negotiating the terms each time.
The client reports high satisfaction in an annual review.
Access: the client brings the practice problems before they are urgent and consults it on what is not yet contracted.
The client pays a recurring fee rather than paying per project.
questions.explanation: The lesson says a satisfied client can still leave and a serial one-off buyer renews out of convenience; access is the raw material that can only be earned, never sold.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: A good service line has three properties, and it is worth testing every candidate line against all three.
The lesson recommends treating output as final without review.
A good service line has three properties, and it is not worth testing every candidate line against all three.
The lesson says only technical staff should act on this.
questions.explanation: A good service line has three properties, and it is worth testing every candidate line against all three.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Setting Up a Consultancy: Legal, Finance, Tooling, and Operations”, why is separating the practice's money from the founder's personal money the first financial act?
options: Because it is required before the practice can file a tax return.
Because mixing the two makes the founder personally liable for business debts.
Because clients will not contract with a practice that pays personal expenses.
Because a practice whose revenue and delivery cost do not land in the same books cannot know what it costs to deliver, so it cannot price.
questions.explanation: The lesson says separation is what makes the operating numbers of utilization, capacity, and margin computable at all.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Governance for Large Engagements”, what does the lesson say about when to escalate a risk?
options: Wait until the committee's next sitting so the escalation is handled in the right forum.
Escalate only after the delivery lead has exhausted their own options.
Escalate once the cost of the risk is large enough to justify the client's attention.
Escalate at the first moment the risk is visible and still actionable, because not escalating is the failure and waiting adds rework, blown dates, and lost trust.
questions.explanation: The lesson describes the cost asymmetry: raising something early costs a short conversation, while waiting costs rework, a blown date, or a dent in trust.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Governance for Large Engagements”, what does a steering committee charter contain, and why does it matter?
options: The written list of decisions that belong to the committee, because without it the committee drifts into being a status meeting with expensive chairs.
The list of attendees and the meeting cadence, because authority follows the calendar.
The escalation thresholds, because those are the only decisions the committee makes.
The delivery plan, because the committee exists to approve the plan.
questions.explanation: The lesson says the test is decisions too big for the delivery team and too frequent or consequential to leave to annual planning.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Compliance and Risk at Enterprise Scale”, what does the lesson say tells the principal that a control on the risk register is actually handling a risk rather than being cosmetic?
options: The risk has been named on the register and reviewed on a schedule.
The risk has a written appetite statement signed by the principal.
The risk appears in the contract and in the client's data-protection terms.
The gap between the inherent exposure and the residual exposure after the control runs.
questions.explanation: The lesson defines that gap as the value of the control, and a control that does not shrink the exposure has not handled the risk.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: The lesson says the opposite: this should always be avoided.
The lesson claims this cannot be verified at all.
The property that makes a standard real is not that the executor runs it without deciding to.
The property that makes a standard real is that the executor runs it without deciding to.
questions.explanation: The property that makes a standard real is that the executor runs it without deciding to.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Capstone, Build a Complete Go-to-Market Plan for Your Own Practice”, why is delivery excellence not enough on its own?
options: Because the market cannot evaluate delivery until the practice is already in the room, so the buyer buys the promise as represented in positioning, offer, and proof.
Because excellent delivery always leads to complacency about quality.
Because referrals dry up once a practice stops billing hourly.
Because enterprise buyers evaluate delivery before they will agree to a discovery call.
questions.explanation: The lesson says weak go-to-market fails because the work is invisible to the people who need it, not because the work is bad.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Long-Term Client Partnerships and Recurring Revenue”, when is a retained client genuinely an asset rather than a comfortable drain?
options: When its recurring revenue grows every quarter without added delivery cost.
When its gross margin exceeds the practice's blended delivery margin.
When its retention rate is above the practice's historical average.
When the stream of value it produces over its lifetime beats the best alternative use of the delivery capability it holds.
questions.explanation: The lesson applies the portfolio lens inside a single account and says the principal must measure rather than assume, because comfort is the most dangerous thing a drain has going for it.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Architecture at Organizational Scale”, what is the central focus?
options: The jump from running agents to running a fleet of them. How to design for many agents at once: the orchestration patterns that keep work moving, the governance layer that keeps it safe, and why control replaces heroics as the unit of success.
A history of the technology and its vendors
A review of unrelated productivity tools
A summary of corporate policy rules
questions.explanation: The lesson is centered on: The jump from running agents to running a fleet of them. How to design for many agents at once: the orchestration patterns that keep work moving, the governance layer that keeps it safe, and why control replaces heroics as the unit of success.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Quality Systems and Certification for Your Practice”, what is the difference between quality control and quality assurance?
options: Control applies to software deliverables and assurance applies to client relationships.
Control inspects an output and decides whether it passes, while assurance shapes the process so defects are not created in the first place.
Control is documented and assurance is informal.
Control is performed by the author and assurance by an external auditor.
questions.explanation: The lesson says the cost of a defect grows with how late it is caught, so moving the catching earlier, or preventing creation, is worth more.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: The lesson claims this cannot be verified at all.
The lesson says only technical staff should act on this.
The reusable starting points for deliverables: the proposal, the discovery brief, the runbook, the report.
The opposite is true: the reusable starting points for deliverables: the proposal, the discovery brief, the runbook, the report.
questions.explanation: The reusable starting points for deliverables: the proposal, the discovery brief, the runbook, the report.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Reference Architectures and Internal Tooling That Compound”, what is the failure mode of accumulated machinery?
options: It outlives its accuracy, so a stale pattern or broken script is worse than absent because it is trusted and followed with confidence.
It grows faster than the practice can document it.
It becomes too specific to the clients it was built for.
It discourages the team from solving new problems from first principles.
questions.explanation: The lesson prescribes a last-reviewed date, an owner, and a scheduled review that asks whether each asset is still true, still used, and still the best way to do this.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Mentorship and Developing Senior Delivery Talent”, a high-potential operator two years from principal is already performing well. Which relationship do they actually need?
options: Mentorship on judgment and sponsorship into the room where the client relationship and the P and L live, because delivering more management is how a firm loses its best people.
More management, because objectives, utilization, and role performance are still unproven.
Coaching on how to work faster within the current role before any new exposure.
All four relationships at once so nothing is missed.
questions.explanation: The lesson says the advanced discipline is triage, and management answers whether someone is doing the job while sponsorship creates the opportunity mentorship turns into capability.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Compliance and Risk at Enterprise Scale”, a practice runs every engagement on one shared agent and one shared memory store, and relies on operators to avoid mixing client material. What control does the lesson name for cross-client bleed?
options: Run each engagement in its own isolated profile with its own memory and state, so separation is a property of the system rather than a rule the operator remembers to follow.
Have operators delete any client material they notice in the shared store.
Keep a written policy that client contexts must never be mixed.
Ask the model provider to guarantee that client data stays separate.
questions.explanation: The lesson says isolation through profiles turns a hard-to-audit human discipline into a verifiable system property.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Mentorship and Developing Senior Delivery Talent”, what distinguishes senior delivery talent from a mid-level operator?
options: More years of experience across a wider range of clients.
A higher utilization rate on client-billable work.
The ability to author the standard rather than only meet it: write the acceptance criteria, place the gate, review someone else's work, and own the estimate and the client relationship.
The habit of escalating fewer problems to the principal over time.
questions.explanation: The lesson says the step up is the move from executing within a framework to owning it, and that nobody becomes ready by being told they are not ready.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Service Lines, Offers, and Packaging”, what is the central focus?
options: How a practice turns capability into something a client can actually buy. The difference between a service line and an offer, why packaging is the principal's real product work, and how productization fixes the worst economics in consulting.
A history of the technology and its vendors
A review of unrelated productivity tools
A summary of corporate policy rules
questions.explanation: The lesson is centered on: How a practice turns capability into something a client can actually buy. The difference between a service line and an offer, why packaging is the principal's real product work, and how productization fixes the worst economics in consulting.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Building Reusable IP and Productized Offerings”, what is the central focus?
options: The difference between an offer and the intellectual property underneath it, why IP is the asset that compounds, and how to turn a repeatable delivery method into a productized offering the practice owns and can sell again without reinventing the scope.
A history of the technology and its vendors
A review of unrelated productivity tools
A summary of corporate policy rules
questions.explanation: The lesson is centered on: The difference between an offer and the intellectual property underneath it, why IP is the asset that compounds, and how to turn a repeatable delivery method into a productized offering the practice owns and can sell again without reinventing the scope.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Compliance and Risk at Enterprise Scale”, a practice treats a client's contractual data-residency requirement as an inconvenient term it can accept as a calculated trade. Why is that the wrong way to treat a compliance obligation?
options: Because residency terms can always be renegotiated down before signing.
Because the practice should carry the risk only if the client agrees in writing.
Because compliance is binary and enforced from outside, so the work is to build a control that meets the obligation rather than decide to accept it as a risk.
Because data-residency rules apply only to the model provider, not to the practice.
questions.explanation: The lesson separates compliance, which is non-negotiable and enforced from outside, from risk, which is a judgment the practice makes for itself.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Mentorship and Developing Senior Delivery Talent”, the lesson says a conversation where the principal explains how they would have handled a situation does not transfer judgment. What does?
options: Handing the operator the written standard and letting them read it until it is memorized.
Letting the operator shadow the principal for a full year before making any decision.
Reviewing the operator's output against the acceptance criteria after each delivery.
A progression of observation, then simulated decisions where the operator commits before the principal reveals their answer, then earned autonomy with a backstop, then judgment with no backstop.
questions.explanation: The lesson says the delta between the operator's committed judgment and the principal's is the actual pedagogical content, and the discipline is to answer with the question rather than the answer.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson’s guidance?
options: The lesson cautions against this in every real-world case.
The opposite is true: a principal sells capacity, wins through leverage, and builds the delivery system rather than the deliverables.
A principal sells capacity, wins through leverage, and builds the delivery system rather than the deliverables.
The lesson claims this cannot be verified at all.
questions.explanation: A principal sells capacity, wins through leverage, and builds the delivery system rather than the deliverables.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Quality Systems and Certification for Your Practice”, what is the hard requirement for a gate?
options: That it happens at the point of delivery so nothing ships unreviewed.
That it is recorded in the quality management system before the work advances.
That it has a named reviewer and a written checklist of criteria.
Separation: the author of the work does not pass their own work, because the person who made the mistake is least likely to see it.
questions.explanation: The lesson says a gate where the author checks their own output is not a gate, it is a hope with a checklist attached.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Reference Architectures and Internal Tooling That Compound”, when should a reference architecture be written down?
options: As soon as the practice decides to offer a class of work, so the first engagement can follow it.
After the second or third time the practice has done that kind of work, because a premature pattern is confident and wrong.
Only after a client has asked for a formal methodology document.
Whenever a competitor publishes an equivalent pattern for the same problem.
questions.explanation: The lesson calls it repetition before codification: by the third time the shape has repeated and the first two rounds of mistakes are already paid for.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Pricing Strategy: From Hourly to Productized to Value-Based”, when is value-based pricing legitimate?
options: When the practice has enough runway to absorb an outcome that does not materialize.

Only when the outcome is measurable against a credible baseline, the client controls enough inputs to make it reachable, and attribution is clean; if any condition fails, decline that model for that engagement.
When the client agrees to a pure contingency fee with no base payment.
When the practice has a proven delivery method and a written standard.
questions.explanation: The lesson says that where any one of those conditions fails, value-based pricing is a trap, and the professional move is to decline or restructure it.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Managing a Client Portfolio Strategically”, what does the lesson say about an account that buys the lowest-margin work and drains senior capability?
options: It should be renewed but staffed with junior operators to protect the margin.
It should be kept, because all revenue is good and churn is the enemy.
It should be converted to an hourly model so the attention cost is visible.
It is a candidate for intentional churn, a deliberate wind-down that reallocates the capability to accounts that will compound.
questions.explanation: The lesson says a practice that cannot name an intentional churn has only accidents and surprises, neither of which is a strategy.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: Your method is not actually captured if it requires the principal's implicit knowledge to run.
The lesson says only technical staff should act on this.
Your method is not not actually captured if it requires the principal's implicit knowledge to run.
The lesson argues this applies only in unrelated settings.
questions.explanation: Your method is not actually captured if it requires the principal's implicit knowledge to run.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson’s guidance?
options: The opposite is true: a principal runs a fleet of agents on many engagements at once, orchestrates the work, and governs it with isolation, permission, and audit.
The lesson claims this cannot be verified at all.
A principal runs a fleet of agents on many engagements at once, orchestrates the work, and governs it with isolation, permission, and audit.
The lesson recommends treating output as final without review.
questions.explanation: A principal runs a fleet of agents on many engagements at once, orchestrates the work, and governs it with isolation, permission, and audit.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Delivery Operations: Utilization, Capacity, and Margins”, a practice shows a healthy delivery margin and a thin practice margin. What does the gap between the two numbers tell the principal?
options: That the practice should raise its prices to restore the practice margin.
That the delivery margin is being overstated in the books.
That the operating layer is carrying too much un-billable overhead for the volume it runs, which is a leak unless that spend is buying IP and slack.
That utilization must be driven higher to fund the difference.
questions.explanation: The lesson says practice margin is what remains after the un-billable operating cost, and the gap between the two margins is the efficiency of the operating layer.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Reference Architectures and Internal Tooling That Compound”, which three properties separate compounding internal tooling from a one-off expense?
options: It is fast, cheap, and automated.
It is documented, approved, and version controlled.
It is reused, it improves with use, and it has a named owner.
It is generic, portable, and independent of any single client.
questions.explanation: The lesson says a tool that is never used again is a one-off expense in reusable-looking clothing, and an unowned tool becomes a liability dressed as an asset.
